sources.news_title: The CEO of Nvidia just resigned over his messy Chinese suspected spy affair. Here's who will probably take over.
sources.text:
The CEO of Nvidia just resigned over his messy Chinese suspected spy affair. Here's who will probably take over.
Jensen Huang lost his AI empire to a geopolitical fling.
The CEO and founder of Nvidia resigned on Thursday morning, following the bombshell revelation that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. With Jensen Huang officially out of the company, the short list of possible successors is going around with some very powerful names on the ticket.
Jensen Huang had what was considered one of the most legendary resumes on the internet. His LinkedIn page listed only two employers. He started out as a dishwasher, busboy, and waiter at Denny’s in 1978. Five years later, he took a decade-long hiatus and then came back in 1993 as the co-founder and CEO of Nvidia.
It’s too early to tell how this chain of events will affect Nvida’s business trajectory and the stability of the AI industry.
After 31 years running his company, bolstered by meteoric growth that made it a household name in the gaming industry and AI, his reign was ultimately cut short, thanks to an extramarital relationship he had with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). Today, Huang officially resigned as the CEO and a board member of Nvidia.
As Huang exits the company, Nvidia appointed a new interim CEO to fill his shoes. Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve in his stead, while Harvey C. Jones will become the company’s first appointed chair of the board.
The night before Huang’s resignation, whispers of possible successors had already made the rounds on the internet, teeming with top talent, familiar faces, and some unexpected surprises.
Polymarket suggested that Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter, was a top contender among traders. However, as of this morning, she sits in third place on the prediction market at only a 3% possibility of securing the spot.
Instead, traders highly favor Ian Buck as the next Nvidia CEO. Buck is the current VP general manager of Hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia. Having invented Compute Unified Device Architecture, which is a software translation platform that enables Nvidia GPUs to train and run advanced AI models, he’s responsible for working with partners to outfit AI data centers with Nvidia’s GPUs. He’s been with the company since 2004 and holds a Ph.D. in computer science from Stanford University.
Far behind Buck in second place, traders think the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, would be a good fit. She’s the executive vice president and chief financial officer of Nvidia with 25 years of experience working with tech giants, including Microsoft, Cisco, and, of course, Nvidia. She holds a bachelor of science degree in finance from the University of Arizona, and she also has an MBA from Southern Methodist University.
RELATED: The AI bubble is about to pop. Here's how to prepare yourself.
Charles Taylor/Getty Images
Outside the prediction markets, the internet floated several other names that would make for interesting replacements. These include powerful people like former Apple CEO Tim Cook, current Apple chief hardware officer and the man behind Apple Silicon chips Johny Srouji, AMD CEO Lisa Su, and Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan.
Blaze News reached out to Nvidia for further comment on the timeline to pick a new permanent CEO, possible investigations from the U.S. government over Alice Huang’s ties to China, and whether there will be any changes to Nvidia’s gaming or AI strategies under its new leadership. We did not receive a response by the deadline, but the company included this message in this morning’s press release:
Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.
It’s too early to tell how this chain of events will affect Nvidia’s business trajectory and the stability of the AI industry, which is already teetering on the edge of collapse. However, after a steep drop in Nvidia’s stock price following the news of Huang’s affair, the company’s valuation is climbing now that an interim CEO has taken over.

sources.news_title: What Jensen Huang’s Nvidia exit means for Washington, Wall Street, and Beijing
sources.text:
JUST IN
It’s a lot to process. On Thursday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. But the implications extend beyond the man and his former company, a critical engine of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom because of its leading-edge computer processors. Below, Atlantic Council experts work through how the personnel shakeup could impact US policy, global markets, and more.
TODAY’S EXPERT REACTION BROUGHT TO YOU BY
- Trisha Ray: Associate director and resident fellow at the GeoTech Center
- Graham Brookie (@GrahamBrookie): Vice president for technology programs and strategy
- Jessie Yin: Associate director with the GeoEconomics Center
- Kenton Thibaut (@kentonthibaut): Senior resident China fellow at the Digital Forensic Research Lab
What it means for Washington
- Nvidia’s advanced chips are “the linchpin of the United States’ leverage in slowing down the AI capabilities of its adversaries,” Trisha explains. But that advantage is also “a single point of failure,” since US export controls are only as strong as the security practices of a handful of companies and people within them.
- Graham sees the incident not as a failure in US intelligence, “but rather a broader failure of coordination and policy execution in how the US government manages national security threats.” With the AI industry vulnerable to intellectual property theft and direct targeting, Washington was “caught flat footed” in risk management and export policy enforcement.
- “As difficult as it is for investors to separate Nvidia’s success from Jensen Huang, it has become nearly as difficult for Washington to separate Nvidia from national security,” Jessie argues. She now sees an opening for Congress to exert greater oversight of the company’s impact on national security and tighten semiconductor export controls. Kenton points to growing momentum in Congress behind chip restrictions such as the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, and the MATCH Act.
- Going forward, Trisha urges greater government scrutiny. “Given how few companies underpin the US AI lead, policymakers should seriously consider direct government oversight,” she argues, such as security clearance–like requirements for company leadership and their major customers, as well as security audits of the exporting entities as a precondition for export licenses.
What it means for Wall Street
- Markets were down slightly today, as Nvidia shares took a hit. Huang’s departure has investors wondering if Nvidia can sustain its dominance without the leader who became a synonym to its success. The company is “going to be unsteady for a while,” Jessie surmises.
- The stakes are higher than Nvidia’s stock price alone. The US economy is already highly exposed to the fortunes of a handful of AI companies that “also happen to be the country’s primary strategic assets in a determinative domain of geopolitical competition,” Graham warns. A failure at one could reverberate across the US economy and national security ecosystem.
- Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has become a major financier of the AI boom—known as “the central bank of AI”—investing in startups and supporting customers that buy its products. Jessie says that the coming months will show “how integral Nvidia has become to AI demand itself.”
Sign up to receive rapid insight in your inbox from Atlantic Council experts on global events as they unfold.
 
What it means for Beijing
- Ahead of a planned meeting next week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Beijing warned Washington earlier today against further technology restrictions, Kenton notes.
- Huang had long opposed strict export controls and was able to speak with both Trump and Xi. “But with Huang out of the picture, there is potentially more political leeway to push forward on a more hawkish approach,” Kenton says.
- Jessie adds that the scandal has “permanently damaged the company’s credibility to push back on export controls,” relationships aside.
- But tougher controls could invite retaliation, Kenton warns. “Beijing could answer new restrictions with curbs on critical minerals or probes of other American firms,” potentially complicating the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting.

sources.news_title: Horny Nvidia CEO No Longer CEO, Possibly Still Horny
sources.text:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who is worth over $100 billion, resigned as CEO on Thursday morning, following an emergency board meeting prompted by several reports that he'd been having various affairs, most notably with someone U.S. officials believe was spying on behalf of the Chinese government.
Nvidia has an unorthodox corporate structure, built around Huang, which largely eschews traditional executive roles in favor of a large council of vice presidents who report directly to Huang, which makes the matter of his succession trickier to game out than it would be in other cases of a CEO doing sex stuff. He'll be succeeded on an interim basis by Colette Kress, formerly the CFO, whom Wired characterizes as one of the few people with a high-level grasp of the company's finances and ties to Wall Street.
A quick recap of how we got here: Nvidia is the single most important hardware technology company in the world, a chip designer that boosted its market cap to more than $4 trillion by making the must-have picks and shovels of the ongoing AI boom. As such, Nvidia is something like a shadow arm of the U.S. government, the latter of which is engaged in the stupidest-ever version of the space race with China over who can build the machine god first. Nvidia wants to sell its best stuff to Chinese companies because it doesn't really care who wins, as long as it makes money for investors, but the Trump administration won't allow it. Meanwhile, the tip-top Chinese AI companies have found ways to smuggle in the best Nvidia chips via third parties mostly based in Southeast Asia.
Over the weekend, the New York Times broke the news that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had personally overseen the drafting of a memo for Donald Trump, detailing Huang's extramarital affair with a woman named Alice Huang (no relation), and that Alice Huang was working as a spy for Beijing. Jensen and Alice Huang were photographed together several times last year in Taiwan after Nvidia signed a $2 billion deal to sell chips to the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International, where Alice Huang worked as an executive. Megaspeed is a spin-off from a Chinese state-affiliated mobile gaming company, pretty obviously retains its ties, and served as a vector for Beijing to import valuable Nvidia chips. The Commerce Department was investigating Megaspeed last year, until Nvidia intervened with the Trump administration and got that investigation squashed. That was the state of things as of Monday afternoon.
Since then, more reporting has surfaced new information about Jensen Huang's affairs and about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed. As to the former, the New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had also been having an affair with Nvidia’s vice president of health Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to him. The Reuters news agency then reported Thursday afternoon that Huang also had a relationship with a second Nvidia employee, though they neither named the employee nor reported any other details. Per the Times, the Powell assignation wasn't super-secret at the highest levels of the company, after someone spotted the two "being affectionate at the hotel" and took a video on their phone. Huang's security detail reportedly got the bystander to sign an NDA, though Nvidia higher-ups reportedly learned what was going on shortly afterward. As to the concept of "Nvidia higher-ups," the Nvidia board is made up of Huang's allies, his family members hold a lot of power, and several Nvidia employees said Huang views the "board primarily as a governance requirement, rather than as an important part of the company's strategy or execution."
More interesting than the in-house affairs is the strange, entangled relationship between Nvidia, Megaspeed, and the governments of Singapore, Taiwan, China, and the United States. Though Nvidia is headquartered in Silicon Valley, most of its chips are produced in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born and where he became something of a celebrity. The island is the global center of chip production; the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company produces "at least 90 percent of the world's most advanced computer chips," per a 2024 Wired story, and consumes 7.2 percent of the island's electricity as of 2022. Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia would spend $150 billion per year in Taiwan, and Nvidia recently announced plans to build a headquarters on Taiwan by 2030. Taiwanese authorities have revoked Alice Huang's entry permit, and they're conducting an investigation into her activities. I will note here that in August, the Taiwanese government charged nine people, including an Nvidia employee, with smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Jensen Huang was first introduced to Alice Huang by her husband and Megaspeed co-executive, the businessman Kang Wei. But more interesting than Kang's connections to Huang is the way Megaspeed set up and ran its Singapore-based operations, as a means of bypassing the U.S. government's export controls against selling chips to China. Megaspeed's anchor customer was Chinese tech giant Alibaba, and per the Journal and the Information, Megaspeed's data centers were not only used to power Alibaba operations: Megaspeed was also smuggling a bunch of chips into China. Singapore investigated Kang and Alice Huang earlier this year, and though Huang was cleared, she was barred from returning to the city-state for lying to investigators.
The Journal also reported that Nvidia switched up the way it reported its revenue shortly after both Singapore authorities and the U.S. Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed. As recently as last summer, Singapore accounted for 22 percent of Nvidia's global business, but once the glare of investigative scrutiny brightened, Nvidia began, per the Journal, "reporting geographic revenue 'based upon the location of the customers' headquarters,' rather than 'customer billing location' as it previously had done." Under the new method, the Singapore line went to zero and got reshuffled under revenue from the U.S. and Taiwan instead. Around this same time, Nvidia cut off its relationship with Megaspeed, and it seems like the former shuffled revenue reporting around in an attempt to hide the sudden cessation of that relationship, which would have raised regulatory eyebrows.
(Speaking of cessations of relationships, the final thing to note here is that Jensen Huang is a signature-jacket guy, which has generated some of the funniest coverage. "Jensen Huang Betrayed the Leather Jacket Community," reads a Times opinion column from Anand Giridharadas, that includes perhaps the first sincere [and sincerely misguided] straight-world invocation of the "leather lifestyle." It's all a bit much, but does serve as a nice on-ramp to this week's fantastic Michael Waters story about the battle for control of the estate of artist Tom of Finland.)
Nvidia shares are down 13 percent over the last five days, including a five percent dip after Huang's resignation. This down period comes within a prolonged broader slump for technology and AI stocks, as several huge companies like Apple and Amazon have cut back on their token usage. If only I had access to Chinese AI stocks. Seems like a good time for those.

sources.news_title: Can NVIDIA Maintain Its Momentum Without Huang?
Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO Amid Foreign Intelligence Inquiry
sources.text:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as president, CEO, and a board member effective immediately on November 12, four days after the company opened an independent investigation into reports that a foreign intelligence operation had targeted him.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while retaining her finance responsibilities, Nvidia announced. The board will consider internal and external candidates for the permanent job.
The leadership change follows reports about Huang’s affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing. China has denied the allegations, and Nvidia’s resignation announcement did not state a reason for his departure.
Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, is the woman at the center of the allegations, the Associated Press reported. She and Jensen Huang are not related. The AP account described suspicions about her ties to the Chinese government; those allegations do not establish that she committed espionage.
Independent review
A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, would oversee the inquiry, Nvidia’s board said in its November 8 statement. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised and that the review would examine all available information.
Jensen Huang acknowledged infidelity in a November 8 email to employees that Nvidia published on its website. He did not identify the other person in that message.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote.
Huang also pledged to cooperate fully with the board’s investigation. His acknowledgment of infidelity did not admit espionage or the disclosure of company secrets.
Kress takes over before earnings
Kress joined Nvidia as executive vice president and CFO in September 2013. She previously held finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft, according to the transition release.
The board also appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair. Jones previously served as CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys.
“The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption,” Jones said in the November 12 release.
Kress said in the same release that the company would continue advancing its work in accelerated computing and artificial intelligence while serving customers, partners, developers and shareholders.
“Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” the company said in the statement announcing his departure.
Provided by Dallas Express

sources.news_title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Abrupt Resignation: A Timeline of How the Scandal Unfolded
sources.text:
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia brings a chaotic week at the chip giant to a dramatic close. His resignation came less than a week after reports emerged that he had an extramarital relationship with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
However, the circumstances surrounding Huang’s downfall began taking shape well before the affair became public. Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, entered the technology industry’s orbit in 2023 after becoming managing director of Singapore-based data-center operator Megaspeed International.
Megaspeed said Thursday that it had complied with U.S. law and was preparing to acquire billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and servers. Over the past two years, Alice Huang—also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le—was photographed and filmed socializing with Jensen Huang. Their connection prompted questions in May from an investor who described the pair’s relationship as “uncomfortably close.”
Here is a timeline of the events leading to Jensen Huang’s unexpected resignation on Thursday.
November 2015
Alice Huang, a former television journalist in China, joins Shanghai Hexi Investment Management as deputy general manager, according to social media posts and records maintained by Simuwang, a Chinese private-equity database. Shanghai Hexi was founded by Kang Wei, who later became her husband, the Wall Street Journal reported.
March 2023
7Road International, a company incorporated in Singapore in 2015, changes its name to Megaspeed. Ownership of the “neocloud” business is transferred to Huang Le Ltd., an entity controlled by Alice Huang, who becomes its managing director.
June 2023
Shanghai Century Litong, a cloud-computing company, is established. A company tied to Alice’s sister, Huang Yu, holds a stake in the business.
October 2023
Nvidia names Shanghai Century Litong a preferred cloud partner, providing the Chinese company with priority access to Nvidia chips, according to The Information.
Around November 2023
Megaspeed’s shares are transferred to another Singapore company, Swiftdata. Alice Huang is no longer listed as a director, according to news outlet Caixin Global.
June 7, 2024
NetThunder, an information-technology company, publishes a social-media photo showing Alice Huang and Jensen Huang with other technology executives at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan.
End of 2024
Megaspeed’s assets surge from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, according to financial filings reviewed by Reuters.
Shipment records covering December 2024 through early 2026, analyzed by short seller Culper Research, indicate that Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported roughly $4 billion in products from a company that assembles equipment containing Nvidia chips.
Early 2025
Alice Huang and Kang Wei jointly promote a Southeast Asian data-center project to Chinese investors. They reportedly told prospective backers they had “no problem securing GPUs”—the graphics-processing units central to Nvidia’s business—and identified Alibaba as a customer, the Financial Times reported.
January 31, 2025
Jensen Huang meets President Trump at the White House, beginning a series of encounters between the two men during Trump’s second term.
February 2025
Singapore opens an investigation into Megaspeed and several other companies over suspected false declarations tied to server purchases and other alleged offenses, according to Bloomberg News.
May 22, 2025
Video captures Jensen Huang and Alice Huang together at a dinner at San Liu Shi Fu restaurant in Taipei, near the time of the Computex technology conference in Taiwan.
READ MORE: Learjet Co-Pilot, 20, Remembered as Gifted Young Aviator
July 2025
Jensen Huang says Nvidia has received approval from the Trump administration to sell its advanced H20 artificial-intelligence chips to China, reversing an earlier administration policy.
“It’s so innovative and dynamic here in China that it’s really important that American companies are able to compete and serve the market here in China,” Huang says.
That same month, Nvidia becomes the first publicly traded company to reach a $4 trillion valuation.
February 2026
Chinese authorities detain Kang Wei, Alice Huang’s husband and business partner, in connection with suspected stock manipulation, sources tell Caixin.
Singapore also bars Alice Huang from re-entering the country after she minimizes her role at Megaspeed during the investigation into the company’s operations, according to a Bloomberg News report.
May 12, 2026
Jensen Huang boards Air Force One in Alaska to join Mr. Trump for a two-day trip to Beijing.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefs Mr. Trump on the counterintelligence risk associated with Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the New York Times reported. The briefing took place before Huang joined the trip and was the second time U.S. intelligence had warned Mr. Trump about the Nvidia chief’s relationship, according to the Times.
September 24, 2026
Jensen Huang attends Mr. Trump’s state dinner at the White House for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
September 29, 2026
Jensen Huang appears at an artificial-intelligence event at the White House, where he signs a set of voluntary AI safety standards amid growing demands for stronger safeguards around the technology.
November 8, 2026
Jensen Huang sends Nvidia employees a message acknowledging that he had an extramarital affair. On the same day, Nvidia’s board announces an independent investigation after reports that the chief executive had become the focus of a “foreign intelligence effort.”
The New York Times reports on Nov. 8 that U.S. government surveillance indicated Alice Huang was transmitting information directly to Beijing.
November 9, 2026
During an unscheduled White House news conference, Mr. Trump says he spoke with Jensen Huang, who told him he did not know about Alice Huang’s alleged connections to Chinese intelligence. Mr. Trump calls the Nvidia CEO an “honorable man” who is “definitely suffering.”
Mr. Trump declines to say when he first learned of the espionage allegations, responding only that it was “not too long ago” and that the information “didn’t make much of an impact on me.”
November 11, 2026
The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia subordinate.
November 12, 2026
Nvidia’s board of directors announces that Jensen Huang has resigned from the company, effective immediately.

sources.news_title: A national-security scandal takes Jensen Huang out just as the AI bills come due
Jensen Huang built the company that powers AI. Now Nvidia must find a way forward without him
Jensen Huang Has Been Ousted as Nvidia CEO
No Plan B, No CEO: The Leadership Lesson Behind Nvidia’s Massive Shakeup
Nvidia interim CEO has Dallas ties including TI stint, SMU degree
Jensen Huang Out at Nvidia; CFO Kress Named Interim CEO
sources.text:
Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as president and chief executive of Nvidia, the company he co-founded in 1993 and built into the dominant supplier of chips for artificial intelligence, after two weeks of reports about his personal relationships that reached into questions of U.S. national security. Nvidia's board said Huang had also left the board, effective immediately, and named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive. The shares fell as much as 14 percent at the open before recovering part of the loss.
The board said Kress, who has been chief financial officer since 2013, will keep that role while serving as interim chief executive and that it has begun a search for a permanent successor that will consider internal and external candidates. It also appointed Harvey C. Jones, a director since 1993 and a former chief executive of the chip-design software company Synopsys, as the first chair in the company's history. "The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Jones said. A regulatory filing showed the board accepted the resignation on Wednesday.
Kress said she was committed to building on the foundation Huang created over 33 years and that the company's focus remains on its customers, partners, developers and shareholders. Nvidia said it will report quarterly earnings on Tuesday, Nov. 17, as scheduled. The board's statement thanked Huang for what it called his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.
The sequence began on Oct. 29, when a newspaper reported that U.S. intelligence had concluded that Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and an executive at a company called Megaspeed, was passing information to Beijing and had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The two are not related. U.S. and Singaporean authorities have reportedly examined whether Megaspeed helped Chinese firms obtain Nvidia processors in possible violation of American export restrictions. According to the same reporting, President Donald Trump was told in late 2025 about the intelligence concerning her alleged activities.
On Nov. 8, Nvidia's board announced that a committee of independent directors, working with outside counsel, would investigate whether the chief executive had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The board said at the time that it had no reason to believe that national security or Nvidia's secrets had been compromised and that it had confidence in Huang. In a message to employees the same day, Huang apologized, acknowledged that he had been unfaithful to his wife, and said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. He did not name anyone. A company spokesperson said then that he was committed to continuing to lead Nvidia.
That position did not hold. On Wednesday, a second report said Huang had also had a relationship with a senior company executive who reports to him, and another said the board was preparing to remove him. The board accepted his resignation that day and announced it the next morning.
Much remains unestablished. Public reporting has not shown what information, if any, was obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed took place. The board's investigation has not released findings. Trump has said Huang told him he did not know that the woman was allegedly a spy. The allegations about espionage come from unnamed U.S. officials cited in news reports and have not been tested in any court or public proceeding.
Markets reacted first to the uncertainty and then to its resolution. Nvidia shares dropped more than 9 percent in after-hours trading on Wednesday on the report that the board was preparing to act, opened sharply lower on Thursday, and then pared the decline to about 7 percent, with the company's market value slipping below $4 trillion. Since last Friday the stock has fallen as much as 19 percent, erasing more than $855 billion in market value, and it is down more than 20 percent over the past month. The broader market held up better, with the major indexes turning higher during the session as traders moved past the announcement.
Analysts focused on governance as much as on the departure. Until Thursday, Nvidia had no board chair, no chief operating officer and no publicly known succession plan, a structure that concentrated authority in a founder who had been the company's only chief executive. One brokerage cut its price target on the stock in half, and an investment manager called the absence of a succession plan a reason to avoid the shares for now. Others argued that a clean break removes the largest source of uncertainty and that the company's products and order book do not depend on one person.
Washington's interest is not limited to the personal conduct. Three Republican chairs of House committees wrote to Huang last week seeking a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 about his interactions with the Megaspeed executive and about Nvidia's safeguards against foreign espionage, saying the reports raised significant national security concerns about China's access to sensitive American technology. Lawmakers have since discussed a subpoena and have asked the administration for materials on the chipmaker's exports to China. House Speaker Mike Johnson called the resignation a big and shocking development and said Huang had done the right thing by stepping down.
The geopolitical stakes explain the attention. Nvidia's most advanced processors are the hardware on which leading artificial intelligence systems are trained, and the United States has restricted their sale to China for several years on national security grounds. Huang was the industry's most prominent voice for keeping access to the Chinese market, warning that losing it would be a tremendous loss for the company. Congress had already scrutinized how restricted Nvidia chips reach Chinese firms through third countries. A chief executive's alleged proximity to a person U.S. intelligence regards as working for Beijing lands directly on that fault line, whatever the investigation ultimately finds.
It also leaves the company's position on China policy without its chief advocate at a moment when Democrats are about to take control of Congress and the administration is weighing how tightly to control chip exports. An interim chief executive with a finance background will have to manage customers, regulators and lawmakers at once, while a board that has just created the post of chair conducts its first search for a leader.
Several markers will show how the transition unfolds. The first is Tuesday's earnings report, where investors will look for any change in guidance and for the tone Kress sets. The second is the Nov. 18 congressional briefing and whether lawmakers still seek Huang's testimony now that he has left. The third is the findings of the board's independent investigation and whether they are made public. The fourth is the timeline and shortlist for a permanent chief executive. The fifth is whether U.S. authorities take any action related to Megaspeed or to chip diversion.
For now, the facts on the record are narrower than the headlines around them. A founder who led one of the world's most valuable companies for 33 years has resigned, the board has installed an interim leader and a chair, and an investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence service is still open. What that investigation concludes will determine whether this is remembered as a governance failure or as something larger.

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang has resigned as the CEO of Nvidia
sources.text:
Jensen Huang has officially resigned as chief executive of Nvidia following a series of revelations regarding his personal conduct and its potential national security risks. The company confirmed that Huang’s departure was accepted by the board on November 11, 2026. In the interim, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will step in to lead the company while the board searches for a permanent successor.
According to The Guardian, the board of directors released a statement that focused on Huang’s history at the company rather than the controversy surrounding his exit. The statement noted, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
TechCrunch noted that the situation escalated after reports that U.S. officials believe Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based firm Megaspeed who is no relation to Jensen Huang, is a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang, who has been married for 40 years, admitted to an affair in an apology message to employees on November 8, 2026. The outlet noted that he did not mention Alice Huang by name but did link his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports,” and said he would cooperate fully with the board’s independent investigation.
Reported chip deals deepened the scrutiny on Nvidia
The Guardian reported that Huang has denied any knowledge of Alice Huang’s alleged ties to the Chinese government. Within days of his apology, TechCrunch noted, The Information reported that Alice Huang and her family had built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips. One of them, Shanghai Century Litong, reportedly facilitated the purchase of $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips, including banned ones.
The scandal grew on November 11, 2026, when The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, reported that Huang had a second extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, per TechCrunch. Powell reports directly to the CEO, and The Guardian noted that the pair were reportedly captured on video being affectionate at a hotel during a company conference in March. Nvidia, Huang, and Powell have not confirmed the report.
The fallout from these reports has been significant for Nvidia’s stock price. Per Reuters, shares opened down 13% on Thursday following the announcement of Huang’s resignation. The Guardian reported that the board had earlier appointed the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship with Alice Huang.
TechCrunch reported that congressional interest is also mounting, as three Republican committee chairmen have requested a closed-door briefing with Huang. Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, has indicated that a subpoena may follow if Huang does not cooperate. President Trump, who called Huang “a fine person” on November 8, wrote on Thursday that Huang “has done a fantastic job” and suggested Apple’s Tim Cook as his replacement, The Guardian reported.
According to Reuters, Colette Kress reached out to staff to provide some stability following the announcements. In a memo to employees, she acknowledged that this has been “an extraordinarily difficult period” and thanked them for their “resilience, professionalism and continued dedication.”
Kress wrote, “I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy.”

sources.news_title: Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim CEO? Longtime exec takes top spot after Jensen Huang resigns
sources.text:
CHICAGO (AP) — With Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, Nvidia is bringing longtime tech executive Colette Kress into the role of interim CEO.
Kress first joined the California-based chipmaker back in 2013. She’s served as Nvidia’s executive vice president and CFO ever since — and will now be stepping into the top post amid the company’s most tumultuous chapter yet.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia over three decades ago and has since become a singular figure in the tech world, resigned after reports of his extramarital affairs came into the spotlight this week. He faced growing calls to step down after The New York Times reported on his relationship with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy — and also late Wednesday, when the outlet and later others found Huang was said to have had another affair with an Nvidia employee.
In a statement about her new interim post as CEO on Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
She added that the company will “continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI.”
Nvidia’s high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. And in her CFO role, Kress was a key architect for financing deals with many of the company’s biggest customers — which today include the likes of other AI titans, such as Anthropic and CoreWeave.
Kress has a long resume in the tech world. Prior to joining Nvidia, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments in a variety of roles, according to her executive bio on the company’s website.
Nvidia did not directly address the affairs in Thursday’s announcement. But over the weekend, the company said it was investigating whether Huang was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort” — and the then-CEO separately apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. China’s Foreign Ministry has dismissed the spying allegations.
By The Associated Press

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang Resigns, Nvidia Shares Tumble
sources.text:
Less than a day after the board of chip-maker Nvidia was said to be mulling the removal of CEO Jensen Huang, Huang has resigned from the company, and its stock price has taken a hit.
Nvidia's board of directors announced early Thursday that Huang had resigned, "effective immediately," following a new report Wednesday that he had conducted a second extramarital affair, this time with a direct report.
The company's CFO and current Executive Vice President Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO, and will do both jobs until a new CEO can be found. Kress has served in her current role since joining the company in 2013.
"Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said in a statement. "We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
Also Wednesday night, the board voted to elect its first-ever chairperson, and that is now venture capitalist Harvey C. Jones, who was formerly CEO of Synopsys. Jones said in a statement that the board has "full confidence" in Kress and the leadership team to continue operations at Nvidia without interruption.
"Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Jones said.
Wall Street seems weary of the transition, and Nvidia's stock price was down over 9% in early trading. As of noon Eastern Time, the stock price had recovered slightly, and was trading at $164.43, down 5.33%. As CBS News notes, this comes after the share price had already lost 9.6% of its value in trading on Monday and Tuesday, following the weekend's report of Huang's affair two years ago with a known Chinese spy.
Nvidia shares were trading at around $228 just a month ago, marking a major loss in valuation. Despite the tumble, the company remains, as of this moment, the second-most valuable company in the world behind Apple, with a market cap of $3.97 trillion.
Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, tells CBS News that while "there is no credible way to put a precise revenue loss" on Huang's departure, "Customers buy Nvidia's computing power, software and networking ecosystem, and those advantages wouldn't disappear with its CEO."
What is clear is that the AI era has seen its first major leadership shakeup — at least since that brief moment in 2023 when OpenAI's board tried to oust Sam Altman.
Following the revelation late last week that Huang had conducted some sort of romantic liaison with Chinese operative Alice Huang (no relation) — which may or may not have led him to convince President Trump to ease restrictions on AI chip sales to China — the New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had also more recently been conducting an affair with Nvidia's vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell.
Huang has not acknowledged the Powell affair, but wrote a memo to company employees over the weekend apologizing for the Chinese spy affair, saying that he had betrayed his wife and children.

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang Resigns: Who Knew of the Alleged Spy Ties?
sources.text:
Nvidia’s founder resigned three days after his board said it had confidence in him. The intelligence at the center of the scandal reportedly reached the White House a year ago. What is on the record, what rests on anonymous sourcing, and why the timing deserves scrutiny.
Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia 33 years ago and built it into one of the most valuable companies in the world, resigned as president, chief executive and director on Wednesday, November 11. According to the company’s Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the board accepted the resignation that day “effective immediately.” Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, 59, is now interim chief executive while keeping her finance job, and longtime director Harvey C. Jones, 73, became the company’s “first-ever Chair of the Board,” as Nvidia put it in a press release dated Thursday, November 12.
The exit capped two weeks of reporting that began on October 29, when The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded a Singapore-linked chip-industry executive close to Huang was passing information to Beijing. Huang has admitted an extramarital relationship with that executive. He has not been charged with anything, and Nvidia’s board said on November 8 it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”
What most coverage misses
Much of the coverage has centered on Huang’s private life. The more consequential questions are about government. If the Times is right, senior officials in the Trump administration held intelligence about a suspected Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS) asset close to the head of America’s most strategically important chipmaker for roughly a year. During that time Huang flew with the President to Beijing while Nvidia pressed for wider chip sales to China. Nobody acted publicly until the story leaked.
Those intelligence claims rest entirely on anonymous sources. They have not been confirmed on the record by any U.S. agency, other outlets have said they could not independently verify related details, and the President disputes part of the timeline. Readers should weigh them accordingly.
Background: Megaspeed and Alice Huang
The woman at the center of the story is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, who is not related to Jensen Huang. She has been associated with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company and Nvidia customer. U.S. and Singaporean authorities have been examining Megaspeed since at least October 2025 over whether advanced Nvidia chips were diverted to China in breach of U.S. export controls. CNBC reports that Megaspeed’s assets grew from about $33 million in 2023 to about $3 billion in 2024, according to corporate filings. In a December 2025 statement, the company said inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department, Malaysia’s trade ministry and Nvidia had found no violations, adding: “We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations.”
RSN reported on November 11 on a separate export-control gap, after a Chinese military-linked university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite a U.S. blacklist. The Megaspeed case is larger in scale. The Information reported that her ties to Jensen Huang helped facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip purchases by Chinese firms; CNBC said it could not independently verify that figure.
The timeline: who knew what, and when
The sequence below separates what is on the record from what is attributed to anonymous officials.
- Late fall 2025 (reported by the NYT, anonymous sources): Trump was first briefed on intelligence about Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and chose to take no action.
- Spring 2026 (NYT, anonymous sources): a memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, circulated to a small number of officials, warned that Alice Huang worked for the MSS. The Times says it was not meant for the President.
- May 2026 (NYT, anonymous sources): on Air Force One en route to Beijing, after Trump added Huang to the delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska, Rubio briefed the President on the issue. The Times describes this as at least the second time in seven months Trump had been told.
- October 29, 2026 (publication): the Times first reports the relationship and the intelligence concerns. An Nvidia statement says “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected.”
- October 30 (on the record): Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs rejects a Wall Street Journal report that Singapore had investigated Alice Huang, stating: “there were no such investigations conducted in respect of Alice Huang.” It confirms that “Investigations into Megaspeed are ongoing.”
- November 3: midterm elections.
- November 5: the Republican chairmen of three House committees, John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford, request a closed-door briefing from Huang, according to TechCrunch.
- November 6 (NYT): the Times reports the existence of the spring memo.
- November 8 (on the record): Huang emails staff: “I was unfaithful to my wife.” The board opens an independent investigation and says it “has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”
- November 9 (on the record): China’s Foreign Ministry calls the spy allegation “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears against China.” Trump defends Huang at the White House.
- November 10: the independent directors retain former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Times publishes its Air Force One account.
- November 11: the Times reports, citing five former employees, that Huang also had a relationship with a subordinate executive. The board accepts his resignation the same day.
Deep dive: the President’s account and the record
Speaking to reporters at the White House on Monday, November 9, Trump said, as CNBC reported: “I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that.” He said he had called Huang “just to see if he’s feeling all right,” and that Huang “said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.” Trump added: “I really believe him.” He also said: “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape.”
The word “then” carries much of the weight. According to the Times account republished by the Honolulu Star-Advertiser, Trump answered “No, I didn’t hear about it then” when asked whether he knew at the time of the May trip. The Times reports he had been briefed on the plane. Asked about the earlier, late-2025 briefing, he said: “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people.” The White House has not released any record that would settle the question either way.
No public reporting so far shows that any agency asked the White House to act against Huang, or to keep him off the Beijing trip, and was refused. The reporting describes briefings and a memo, not a rejected recommendation. If such a request existed, it would change the story. Without one, “the President was told and did nothing” remains a characterization, not a documented decision.
The governance question
Nvidia’s board moved from expressing confidence in Huang on November 8 to accepting his resignation on November 11, a span of three days. Until this week the company had never had a board chair, and no successor was in place: the board named no permanent replacement. Kress now holds both the chief executive and chief financial officer roles, and the company says it will consider “internal and external candidates.”
The market has priced in the uncertainty. The Associated Press reported that Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on November 9 and had lost roughly 11% since the previous Wednesday. TechCrunch reported a further drop of about 8% in after-hours trading on November 11. CBS News put the stock down nearly 5%, at around $165.25, by midday Thursday. Nvidia still plans to report third-quarter results on November 17.
Analysis: why did it break now?
The following is RSN analysis, not established fact. The first Times story ran on October 29, five days before the midterms, so the claim that officials waited until after the election does not fit the record. What did come after November 3 was the escalation: the memo story on November 6, the Air Force One account on November 10, and a steady flow of details that appear to come from people with access to classified briefings.
The timing also lines up with the President’s next trip to China. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting is set for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen. According to the Times, Trump has said Huang will not accompany him and that he does not plan to raise the matter with Xi. A drip of anonymous disclosures that removes the country’s leading advocate of chip sales to China from a summit with Xi Jinping would suit officials who oppose those sales. There is no public evidence that the leaks were coordinated, and that reading should be treated as opinion.
Conservatives have seen this pattern before. During the Russia investigation, a series of anonymous intelligence leaks shaped public opinion for months before the underlying claims were tested, and several did not hold up. That history does not prove the Huang reporting wrong. The pattern is similar, though: classified material is released selectively, the public cannot check it, and the targets cannot answer it in full. Washington’s record of soft responses to Chinese intelligence activity, which RSN criticized as far back as 2014 in “China, Hacking and Murder,” is the opposite risk, and both deserve attention.
Counter-arguments
The President’s case. Trump has said Huang told him he did not know of any intelligence link, that he believes him, and that Huang “built a great company, American company.” Nvidia’s own board said it had no reason to believe secrets were compromised. Huang’s defenders argue that an American firm leading the world in artificial intelligence (AI) hardware is a national asset, and that removing its founder over unproven allegations helps Beijing more than Washington.
Beijing and Singapore. China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on November 9, as the AP reported: “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.” Beijing has an obvious interest in denying it. Singapore’s government has no such motive, and it has stated on the record that it did not investigate Alice Huang.
The critics. On the other side, Sen. Elizabeth Warren said Huang’s departure does not end the matter and that Huang, Nvidia’s executives and its board “still owe Congress answers about the company’s compliance with U.S. export controls,” CBS News reported. House Republicans have also pressed for a briefing, and, according to TechCrunch, Rep. Moolenaar said on Fox Business that Huang would likely be subpoenaed if he declined.
What is established, disputed and not established
Established (on the record):
- Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director; the board accepted it on November 11 (SEC Form 8-K).
- Colette Kress is interim chief executive; Harvey C. Jones is the first board chair.
- Huang admitted an extramarital relationship in a November 8 email to staff.
- The board opened an independent investigation led by Joon H. Kim of Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.
- Singapore says investigations into Megaspeed are ongoing and that it did not investigate Alice Huang.
- China’s Foreign Ministry denies the spy allegation.
Disputed:
- Whether Trump was told about the intelligence before or during the May Beijing trip. The Times says yes; the President says he “didn’t hear about it then.”
- Whether Megaspeed diverted restricted chips to China. The company denies it; investigations continue.
Not established:
- That Alice Huang is an MSS asset. This rests on anonymous U.S. sources; no charges have been filed and no agency has said so on the record.
- That any Nvidia or U.S. government secret was compromised.
- That any official recommendation to act on the intelligence was rejected.
- That the leaks were coordinated or timed for political effect (RSN analysis only).
The next checkpoints are close together: Nvidia’s earnings on November 17, the APEC summit on November 18 and 19, and the House committees’ push for Huang’s testimony. Any of them could move the story from anonymous claims to the public record.
Sources: Nvidia Form 8-K, November 11, 2026; Nvidia newsroom: CEO transition, board statement (Nov. 8), Huang email (Nov. 8), independent directors (Nov. 10); Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs / Singapore Police Force, Oct. 30; New York Times via Honolulu Star-Advertiser; CNBC, Nov. 9; CNBC on Megaspeed; Associated Press, Nov. 9; TechCrunch timeline; CBS News; CGTN on APEC 2026 dates.

Good Morning, Portland! This morning I have watched an AI drama where aliens keep humans as pets (but still get cats for them) and tried to add myself to my own airdrop contacts instead of writing Good Morning, News! Don’t be like me; read the dang news!
IN LOCAL NEWS:
• The holiday season is upon is. The Mercury’s Holiday Issue is here to support you through this dire time. It’s got cozy bars, gift ideas, and “A Holiday Survival Guide (for the End Times).” Read it all online, or find this prized stallion out on stands around the city.
• ABOUT WEATHER: Remember that torrential rain from Monday and Tuesday? Not today! But Friday? Get your toilet rat a cheeseboard because Big Rain is back on Friday.
• Will you brave the torrents in the name of art and fun? Mercury Music Editor Starly Lou Riggs has some concerts they think are worth re-waterproofing your booties for… SUCH AS iconic Reiko Takahashi of Japanese City Pop fame, LA-based Agriculture’s post-black metal, Dev Lemons’ campy pop performance, and more.
• If I’ve said it once, I’ve said it 1000 times! Don’t leave your numerous unique miniature horse figurines in your car downtown overnight! A release from Portland police says that a woman reported a Sunday night theft from her parked, unoccupied rental car in the area of SW Harvey Milk and SW 10th. She also told police she’d heard someone was passing out horse figurines after the theft. Portland Police Central Precinct Neighborhood Response Team (NRT) identified a suspect selling or handing out horse figurines to others, and on Wednesday, they arrested him. Terrible news for news interns being sent to purchase illicit tiny street horses, but great news for the original owner.
• The Oregonian just dropped this gorgeous deep dive into the state’s history of permitting families to refuse medical care for their children due to spiritual beliefs. In 1999, Oregon’s legislature removed it as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment, but those whose religion forbids medical intervention still struggle with the choice. This investigative piece by Noelle Crombie isn’t a gotcha crime story, but it does include a charismatic preacher named Walter White and a father who faced widespread community shunning for taking his young son to the hospital—an action which saved his son’s life.
IN NATIONAL & INTERNATIONAL NEWS:
• If you’re reeling from the news of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang having an extramarital affair with an alleged spy, buckle up. Because Huang resigned Thursday morning, following Wednesday revelations that he also conducted an affair with his company’s vice president of health care—an executive who reported to him. 😬 And I’m with you, why do we care about this guy’s weird affairs? Well, this is currently news because Nvidia is set to invest $10 billion in Anthropic’s Initial Public Offering (IPO), which had been pushed back before, but was set to go ahead on November 19. On a larger scale, the business world has been focused on AI technology as the next big thing and processing chips are a major part of that. PJ Vogt’s podcast Search Engine just churned out an episode titled “What Was Jensen Huang Thinking?” wherein Vogt asserted: “Every other podcast this week is gonna tell you this is a story about sex because they think you think sex is exciting.” Vogt thinks this is about an export control rule change in 2022 that banned US companies from selling their most cutting edge chips to China, which locked China from chips that their AI companies really wanted. So now… Nvidia needs a new CEO, and tech pundits stayed up all night making their vision boards. Let’s dream, people.
• Mississippi has elected a senator from the Democratic party for the first time since 1982, according to the latest returns, which put Scott Colom over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by 4,669 votes on Wednesday. Colom also represents the first Black senator to represent the state since 1881. CNN reports that Colom, a local district attorney, centered his campaign on affordability issues, labeling Hyde-Smith “Cindy High Prices.”
• A three-story building collapsed in Brooklyn on Wednesday. The New York Times reports that the structure crumbled into a large hole created by an adjacent construction site. Further reporting has thus far revealed that the Department of Buildings had previously ordered the construction site’s property owner to halt demolition in March, due to inadequate protection for nearby properties. Upon re-inspection, the department found that a previously standing one-story structure had been leveled anyway. The department issued a $10,000 fine for the violation, but by August the order to hold construction was fully lifted. At this time, it appears that two people have died and 17 were injured by the collapse, with four of those injuries considered critical.
• An Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier chastised Pete Hegseth on Wednesday after the defense secretary and the group he was with broke into laughter at the solemn site. Hegseth, his wife, and a few others had been posing for photos and chatting on the memorial’s steps as part of a Veteran’s Day visit with President Trump. Located in Arlington National Cemetery, the tomb represents remembrance for military members killed in battle who remain unidentified. Arlington Cemetery famously prohibits yelling and/or making any other “boisterous” or “unreasonably loud” noise.
• On Tuesday, the US House blocked an effort to impeach Pete Hegseth, losing the vote by just seven and allowing a Republican majority to shelve the idea. It turns out that 11 Democratic party members were absent from that vote! And what’s their excuse for missing it? The majority of them blamed traffic. 😬
• A retired US circuit judge Richard A. Posner died Tuesday at age 87. Posner is an interesting figure because he was most-cited legal scholar in the second half of the 20th century by a wide margin. NYT reports that a 2000 study conducted by Fred R. Shapiro showed Posner beating runner-up Ronald Dworkin by a factor of almost two.
• Nothing can prepare you for how dark this Ben Harkins stand-up set gets before the pure crowd candy of his “Men’s Mental Health” song.

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang, a global salesman for artificial intelligence, resigns from Nvidia after affair
sources.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, capping a spectacular downfall for a poster boy of the artificial intelligence boom whose exit following reports of extramarital affairs now thrusts the chipmaker into an uncertain future.
After a dizzying series of headlines about Huang’s infidelity and ties to an alleged Chinese spy, his departure sets off a scramble to find a permanent replacement to lead the multitrillion-dollar colossus that grew from obscurity to a perch between Apple and Microsoft at the top of the S&P index.
The resignation sent shares of Nvidia plummeting 14% at the opening bell, before stabilizing. The stock closed down about 4% Thursday as investors pondered the lawsuits, investigations, likely corporate jockeying and the resilience of a market driven by the gains of a few tech giants.
“Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself,” said Asa Hiken, senior analyst for research firm eMarketer, reflecting fears of wider implications and the possibility of an AI bubble.
The company named Colette Kress, the executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim chief executive. She became CFO in 2013, overseeing the company’s global finance operations. Before that, she worked for three years at Cisco and spent 13 years at Microsoft.
Nvidia had no succession plan to prepare for the possibility of the departure of Huang, who was synonymous with Nvidia for more than 30 years in much the same way Steve Jobs embodied Apple. Nvidia said its board would consider internal and external candidates to replace him.
In a statement Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
The board of directors said Thursday it had also named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor.
Drumbeat of scandals grew louder
Huang, 63, is one of the world’s wealthiest people, with a personal fortune that Forbes estimates at more than $150 billion. He is the single largest individual shareholder of Nvidia stock.
A drumbeat of scandals around him had grown louder in recent weeks after The New York Times reported Huang's relationship with a woman the paper said U.S. officials had concluded was a Chinese spy who was recruited to influence California-based Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.
The discovery set off alarms as high as the White House.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating but remained complimentary of Huang on Thursday, saying he “has done a fantastic job.” Like many top tech CEOs, Huang is close to Trump, who has hosted him at the White House and on Air Force One, and awarded him a National Medal of Science.
Nvidia's board announced an investigation into the allegations on Sunday, but said it remained confident in Huang's leadership. Then pressure compounded late Wednesday after reports surfaced of another alleged affair by Huang, this time with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. Reuters reported Thursday that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, citing unidentified sources.
The company has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or its secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Nvidia is due to report earnings Tuesday.
Lawmakers still want to question Huang
After Huang’s exit, U.S. lawmakers were still insisting on questioning him about his interactions with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang and the company’s security protocols against espionage.
“Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk,” Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.
Rep. Brian Mast, chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, said the committee was in contact with Huang’s team as recently as Wednesday night after putting in an initial request for an interview on Nov. 5. Mast said Huang would receive a subpoena to compel his appearance, if necessary.
Alice Huang, the suspected spy at the center of the scandal, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair but did not identify her.
The two are not related.
Megaspeed faced allegations last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
Singaporean authorities said Thursday that they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded that there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country.
China denies attempting to ensnare executive
China has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI, and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump’s approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chips to China.
Megaspeed said Thursday that it has cooperated with the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which handles enforcement of national security restrictions on technology exports, and was ready to “cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority.”
The company said it has hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a “comprehensive census” of its computer chips and to verify its export controls.
“Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws,” it said.
Apart from questions over national security, Megaspeed’s finances also have drawn attention. Its total assets soared roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost $3 billion, according to Singapore corporate records.
Revenue surged to over $294 million in 2024 from none in 2023.
What comes next for Jensen Huang is unclear, though another tech mogul, Elon Musk, said on X that it “would be an honor” to hire him.
At a time of growing alarm about AI's potential risks, Huang has been a voice of optimism on the technology’s potential. His climb to the top of the corporate world started with an idea born in an unglamorous setting.
Huang and two other engineers gathered in 1993 at a Denny’s in San Jose, California, where they discussed building a computer chip that would make graphics for video games faster and more realistic.
That conversation led to the founding of Nvidia.
Associated Press writers Barbara Ortutay in San Francisco, Mae Anderson in New York, Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong and Kevin Freking and Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.
