sources.news_title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as scandal shakes AI industry | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as scandal shakes AI industry
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down today after revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll.
Huang’s exit caps a tumultuous week for Nvidia, one of the major engines behind the AI boom, and could have far-reaching consequences for U.S. chip export policy and the broader AI ecosystem, given the ex-CEO’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market, as well as his close ties with President Donald Trump.
The crisis has threatened to implicate some Trump administration members, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is facing growing questions over the administration’s oversight of chip sales to China, particularly as both he and Huang pushed for relaxing those sales despite scrutiny from longtime China hawks in both parties. The Commerce Department did not immediately comment.
RELATED STORY: Chinese AI firms rush to secure overseas Nvidia computing capacity
Senior White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out, two people familiar with the situation told Reuters today.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Lutnick’s future. Earlier in the day, a White House official said President Donald Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position.”
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Huang’s departure threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped shape by pouring Nvidia’s swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry’s biggest labs. The surge in AI computing demand drove a sevenfold increase in Nvidia’s shares through early October, pushing its market value at one point to nearly $6 trillion.
Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, considering both internal and external candidates, the company said today.
The departure has also ignited speculation over who will ultimately lead the company, long associated with the leather-jacket-wearing Huang, who co-founded Nvidia more than three decades ago.
Kress and longtime Nvidia engineer Ian Buck had emerged as the leading internal candidates among investors and analysts even before Huang’s departure.
Nvidia shares were down about 4.8%, paring earlier losses. Shares of rivals AMD and Broadcom rose about 6% each.
Huang, Nvidia’s fourth-largest shareholder with a 3.61% stake, will also leave the board. Nvidia named former Synopsys CEO and longtime director Harvey Jones as its first board chair.
“The Board, Estaff (executive staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period,” Kress wrote in a memo to employees, adding that the company will host a meeting on November 18.
Kress was gathering Nvidia’s executive team at its headquarters today, CNBC reported, adding that Huang had agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving.
Huang has hired law firm Paul Weiss, the New York Times reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. It was not clear what the firm had been retained to do, the report said.
The company has not commented beyond its statement announcing Huang’s resignation.
Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
The New York Times also reported Wednesday that Huang had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.
While Kress offers investors a familiar hand after 13 years as CFO, analysts have pointed to Buck as a potential longer-term candidate because of Nvidia’s reliance on technical leadership. The veteran engineer helped develop its crucial CUDA software platform and now leads its hyperscale AI products.
“The risk is not that Nvidia suddenly loses its technology roadmap … that roadmap is largely visible for the next several years. The risk is execution. Jensen has been the chief conductor of an extraordinarily complex system,” said Michael Feldman, portfolio manager at ClearBridge Investments.
“In a world with real bottlenecks, that coordination is a competitive advantage in itself.”
Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off.
Trump said on Sunday that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country” and that the Nvidia chief had told him he had no idea the Chinese woman he had an affair with was a spy.
Trump today suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over as Nvidia’s CEO.
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson said it was “critically important for right successor to be chosen to replace Huang,” noting there was a growing consensus in Congress on limiting exports of semiconductor chips to China.
For years, Nvidia was best known to gamers chasing top-tier graphics. But its chips’ ability to perform many calculations at once has made them the oil of the AI boom and a strategic prize in the U.S.-China race to dominate the technology. It also made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company.
That turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who ask him to sign books, posters and sometimes even their bodies.
The scandal preceding Huang’s departure unfolded over more than a year, beginning with an October 2025 New York Times report linking him to Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a coveted official Nvidia cloud partner with priority access to its chips.
Subsequent reports said U.S. intelligence officials believed Alice Huang was acting on behalf of Chinese intelligence. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.
Washington has also investigated Megaspeed over suspicions it helped China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under U.S. export controls, according to media reports.
Separately, Bloomberg News reported today that the U.S. Justice Department was investigating Alice Huang over whether entities linked to her were involved in efforts to smuggle Super Micro Computer products to China, citing a person familiar with the matter.
A spokesperson for the Manhattan U.S. Attorney’s office declined to comment on the Bloomberg report. The office previously charged three people associated with Super Micro, including its co-founder, with helping smuggle at least $2.5 billion of U.S. AI technology to China in violation of export laws. Super Micro did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Earlier, the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs said Singapore police had been investigating Super Micro as part of a wider probe into Megaspeed and Alice Huang. The police had reached out to the FBI and the Justice Department for help and had received “limited information or assistance,” the ministry said.
Earlier this month, Nvidia’s board launched a probe, led by independent directors with outside legal counsel, into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. It also expressed confidence in him at the time.
The controversy escalated on Wednesday when the New York Times reported Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported to him.
Additional reporting by Luc Cohen, Arpan Varghese and Estelle Shirbon.

sources.news_title: Nvidia’s Huang resigns, Bombs threats grip Europe, Spain’s PM gets boost before election
sources.text:
Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of Nvidia
The co-founder of the chipmaking colossus resigned on Thursday, just days after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang’s exit sends shockwaves through the tech industry and the wider geopolitics attached to it. He was, personally, the force that made Nvidia a dominant player in AI, both as an elite chipmaker and data center investor. His exit could rattle investor sentiment in the AI boom and raises the question of whether Nvidia can maintain its leading position in the sector. If not, competition for its market share will be brutal (and political) among both American and Chinese firms. What’s more, we don’t know whether Huang’s affair compromised US national security. This all highlights a new kind of risk: tech companies exert almost state-like power in some areas of global politics, but they often depend heavily on their CEOs, whose vulnerabilities or indiscretions can quickly rattle the world.
Mysterious bomb threats continue to rattle Europe
Hundreds of schools across Italy were evacuated on Wednesday due to hoax bomb threats emailed to over 6,000 schools. These are just the latest in a wave of hoax threats impacting Europe. Last week, airports in several countries, including the Czech Republic, Denmark, and Ireland, received multiple bomb threats that grounded dozens of flights and, in some cases, forced emergency landings. Yet, no explosives were found. Dozens of threats were also made to schools in Northern Ireland and Scotland yesterday. And once again, no bombs were discovered. European authorities have yet to say who they think is responsible, though they have said the threats appear to be coordinated. The incidents come amid growing concerns in Europe over hybrid attacks from Russia and Iran, particularly after hackers that French officials said were affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted refrigeration systems in cyberattacks across France, Belgium, and Luxembourg.
Spain’s PM gets a big win before elections
Just one day after Spanish workers staged the country’s largest general strike in over a decade, Pedro Sánchez scored a major political victory. Parliament passed a much-anticipated housing reform earlier today that caps rent, includes a temporary ban on evictions, and imposes restrictions on corporate ownership of rental properties. Sánchez’s government has been plagued by corruption scandals and low approval ratings, and he made a risky gamble this summer by calling snap elections amid widespread anger over housing costs. Since then, he has tried to position himself as a champion of housing reform, and the new measures give him a real victory to tout. Meanwhile, the leader of the conservative People’s Party, which has been leading Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party in the polls, vowed to repeal the reforms if elected, which might also help Sánchez ahead of the election at the end of the month.

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang Resigns As CEO of Nvidia Following Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy
sources.text:
Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO, Social Media Reacts
Jensen Huang Resigns As CEO of Nvidia Following Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy
CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO.
Share the post
Share this link via
Or copy link
- Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia CEO following revelations of affairs, including with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent.
- The scandal triggered a 10% stock drop that erased $750 billion in market value, forcing the board to act.
- Trump administration faces scrutiny for not disclosing known concerns about Alice Huang's alleged ties to Beijing before inviting Huang to China.
It never fails; a powerful man can’t keep it in his pants. Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, is the latest example of a CEO caught cheating on his wife, but this time there are national security implications.
Following reports of Nvidia’s board of directors having discussions on how to deal with its philandering CEO after reports surfaced of Huang having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Huang has decided to step down.
Huang co-founded the chipmaker 33 years ago and helped build it into a $4 trillion company that helped push the artificial intelligence boom.
CFO Colette Kress has been named interim CEO.
“The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption,” said board chair Harvey Jones in a release.
Jensen Huang Also Had A Second Affair
Huang’s resignation also comes on the heels of reports that he had another affair with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who joined the company in 2008 and heads the company’s healthcare business.
As expected, the news of Huang’s affair sent Nvidia’s stock tumbling; it plunged over 10% and erased -$750 billion in market cap. So you know once that happens, the board of directors, who at one point were still backing Huang, are now saying, like, whoa, our bottom line is taking a hit here.
But it’s Huang’s affair with the alleged Chinese spy that is raising major red flags due to its national security implications.
Last month, the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence services believed the woman involved in the alleged affair, Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, was possibly acting as an intelligence agent and reporting back to the ruling party in Beijing.
Huang, 63, did apologize on Sunday for being “unfaithful to my wife,” and also pushed back on allegations that he compromised national security or divulged Nvidia secrets during pillow talk.
Also caught up in this mess is President Donald Trump, who developed a close bond with Huang, who, along with Nvidia, has contributed to Trump’s political and civic initiatives.
Huang became one of the loudest voices on the U.S.’s AI policy and, at the same time, pushed Nvidia’s interests, specifically lobbying for chip exports to China.
This past May, Huang joined Trump on a trip to China, and while on stage at an All-In Summit to discuss AI safety and regulation, the President called in, and Huang put him on speakerphone, with Trump telling Huang and the audience, “I’m with you all the way.”
Donald Trump Claims He Didn’t Know About Huang Sleeping With An Alleged Spy
As expected, Trump claimed he didn’t know about the allegations when he invited Huang to join him on the trip to China, even though the Washington Post reports that U.S. officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and CIA Director John Ratcliffe, briefed the administration on concerns about Alice Huang’s ties to the Chinese government.
So if Trump thinks this will go away, he better think again because when Democrats take over the government in January, you can most definitely they will look into this matter as part of their oversight duties.
It looks like both Trump and Huang could be in some serious trouble.

sources.news_title: How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
sources.text:
How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
If I'd told you this time last week that Jensen Huang was about to leave Nvidia, you would not have believed me.
The man who co-founded this enormously successful AI chip company, working tirelessly to build it from the ground up and steering it through some disastrous times with endless energy and ruthless determination, has ultimately been undone by his own love life.
It's an extraordinary tale and a strangely old fashioned one for a tech firm with its sights set on the future.
It spawned a plethora of viral memes, seeing Huang as the man caught by the Coldplay kiss-cam with a married colleague, or singing along to George Michael's classic hit about betrayal, Careless Whisper.
Both were ironically AI-generated using the very tech he was helping to build.
This week I met two Silicon Valley execs and I asked them how they were processing the news - "in memes", was the response.
But they didn't seem to think Huang would be forced out by his alleged adultery.
The stakes were too high, they said, the entire AI industry relies too heavily on Nvidia chips to break a winning formula.
In as many words, "the Valley" was on his side.
But that was before rumours of a second affair surfaced, this time with a colleague, and the board decided he had gone too far.
His behaviour suddenly cast him in a different light: a man who could make bad decisions and cover them up.
Long hours and competitive spirit
Huang always made a point of standing out from the crowd.
During the coronavirus lockdowns, he streamed keynote speeches from his kitchen (which gained internet fame in its own right, but were later revealed to have been AI-generated).
He is rarely seen without a leather jacket – he has joked that he only owns one suit, and he borrows his daughter's partner's tie.
Huang rubbed shoulders with the elite, with a network including Donald Trump, Elon Musk and King Charles.
The last time I saw him was at St James' Palace last year, where he was receiving the prestigious Queen's Prize for Engineering.
I was told he would not talk to the press - but he wandered over by himself and we spent about 10 minutes having a chat while press officers hovered nervously in the background. He was articulate and optimistic about the progress of AI and the UK's role in it.
For many people, Huang was Nvidia. He had as many as 200 people directly reporting to him.
He expected high standards – in his book about its inner workings, the Nvidia Way, author Tae Kim wrote the office hours were long.
Huang's feedback could be both brutal and public, and he thought nothing of pointing out individuals' mistakes in all-staff meetings.
Now it is his own shortcomings which are on very public display, and he has been forced into a brutal ending of his own career.
Nvidia without Huang
Colette Kress, who takes over for now, will be a familiar face internally and that must feel reassuring to some at Nvidia.
She's worked at the company for 13 years and for those who follow its considerable finances, she is often present on earnings calls. She is a billionaire in her own right and a high-flying tech executive.
But she's not an engineer and Nvidia's products are highly technical.
She will have to convince investors that it is business as usual for Nvidia, that the innovation for which it is renowned can continue at its existing pace, and that the top talent won't leave with Huang.
A wobbly Nvidia would be bad news for the entire AI industry because its ever-advancing chips drive the most powerful AI models, and it's also regarded as something of a central bank, loaning money to other firms.
As for Huang himself, we assume for now that the investigation into his relationship with the woman accused of being a Chinese spy will continue, and the results of that may well determine what he does next.
He probably won't be short of offers despite his conduct – and I expect Nvidia's rivals can't believe their luck that their formidable rival has taken himself out of the game. Elon Musk has already said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.
It's important though to remember that even if Huang turns out not to have betrayed his company or his country, he still betrayed his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang.
And for her, it's not a story of tech, temptation and trillion-dollar-valuations.
It's a painfully personal matter.

sources.news_title: Nvidia Board Removes CEO Jensen Huang Following Espionage Allegations
sources.text:
The board of directors at Nvidia, the dominant player in the artificial intelligence chip market, announced on Thursday that Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang is stepping down. The decision follows an internal investigation launched by the company after media reports alleged that Huang had a relationship with a client who, according to U. S. intelligence officials, was recruited by China's top spy agency. While Nvidia has confirmed the leadership change, the company has not independently verified the specific allegations regarding espionage, and China's foreign ministry has dismissed the claims as baseless.
The removal of Huang, who co-founded Nvidia 33 years ago and led the company to a valuation of more than $4 trillion, marks a significant shift in corporate governance for the world's most valuable tech firm. The board appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and stated that it would conduct a full search for a permanent successor, considering both internal and external candidates. This institutional move was triggered by the disclosure of Huang's relationship with an executive at a Singapore-based company purchasing Nvidia chips, as well as reports of a second affair with a subordinate. The company's share price fell sharply on Wednesday following reports of the second relationship.
The timeline of the company's response indicates a rapid escalation from media exposure to board action. In late October, the New York Times reported that U. S. intelligence officials believed Huang's associate had been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on him and potentially influence policy. Following these reports, Nvidia launched an investigation. On Sunday, Huang admitted to extramarital affairs in an email to staff and pledged cooperation with the inquiry. The board's Thursday decision to remove him from the CEO role represents the culmination of this internal process, prioritizing corporate stability over the CEO's long-standing tenure.
The situation has drawn immediate political attention, particularly regarding the timeline of government awareness. Representative Yvette Clarke, a senior member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, expressed concern that senior Trump administration officials may have known about the allegations for weeks or months. Clarke stated that the White House's awareness is "very disturbing” and suggested that the matter, including the extent of government knowledge and Huang's relationship with the alleged agent, would likely be subject to congressional investigation when Democrats take control of Congress in January. Despite the leadership vacuum, Nvidia remains committed to its operational schedule and plans to report quarterly earnings on Tuesday. Analysts note that while Huang's strategic vision transformed Nvidia's niche in graphics processing units into the backbone of the AI industry, his departure leaves the company without its primary architect, a position for which no clear public succession plan had been established.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after his extramarital affair raised national security concerns, in a spectacular downfall for the longtime head of the chipmaker, a vital player in the artificial intelligence boom.

The company named Colette Kress as interim Chief Executive. She is the current Executive Vice-President and Chief Financial Officer.

Kress took over the role as Nvidia’s chief financial officer in 2013, overseeing the company’s global finance operations. Before that, she worked for three years at Cisco and spent 13 years at Microsoft.

Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor.
Shares of Nvidia tumbled 14 per cent at the opening bell Thursday, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq slid 1.5 per cent.
Nvidia’s board had gathered to discuss Huang’s future after revelations about his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International suspected of being a Chinese government agent. The two are not related.
In its first statement since the scandal broke, Megaspeed said Thursday that it takes its obligation to comply with US export control laws “extremely seriously.” The company prominently touts a partnership with Nvidia on its website. The two are not related.
Details about Huang’s affair with the former Megaspeed executive are unclear.
“Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” said the statement signed by its chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan.
Nvidia has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or its secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Last month, the Times reported that US intelligence agencies discovered that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang - and determined that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that the FBI was investigating.
Megaspeed faced allegations last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.
Singaporean authorities said Thursday that they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded last year that there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime but barred her from returning to the country.
China has denied that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, who heads one of the world’s most valuable companies. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump’s approval to sell its H200 chips to China.
Megaspeed said Thursday that it has cooperated with the US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which handles enforcement of national security restrictions on technology exports, and was ready to “cooperate fully with any other relevant US government authority.”
It said it has hired a US law firm to conduct a “comprehensive census” of its computer chips and to verify its export controls.
“Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable US laws,” it said.
Apart from questions over national security, Megaspeed’s finances also have drawn attention. Its total assets soared roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost USD 3 billion, according to Singapore corporate records.
Revenue surged to over USD 294 million in 2024 from none in 2023.

sources.news_title: The Nvidia mess should end the era of unregulated AI
sources.text:
Skip to content
The Nvidia mess should end the era of unregulated AI | Editorial
Jensen Huang’s resignation after acknowledging an affair with a suspected Chinese spy makes the Trump administration’s irresponsible approach to the technology that much more untenable.
Even among a legion of Big Tech sycophants, Jensen Huang had stood out for his capacity to flatter Donald Trump into giving him what he wanted. It turned out that Huang, the perpetually leather-swathed chief executive of Nvidia, was not impervious to such motivated means of persuasion himself — and he has paid a devastating price for it.
Huang resigned Thursday as the head of the microchip giant, days after acknowledging an extramarital affair with a Singapore-based tech executive known as Alice Huang, who is believed to be a Chinese spy. The revelations about their relationship would have been awkward for anyone, but it was particularly so for the man who successfully lobbied the president to ease restrictions on exporting his company’s AI-enabling chips to the agent’s alleged handlers.
Further complicating matters for Huang was a report by the New York Times late Wednesday that he had engaged in a second affair with a subordinate at the company.
» READ MORE: Bike protest of Jewish businesses was indefensible, and it must be condemned | Editorial
The scandal seems to have done what all the artificial intelligence industry’s warnings about its own destructive potential somehow did not. It triggered a sell-off of Nvidia stock, federal investigations and renewed questioning of the headlong, government-assisted rush to develop a dangerous, ill-understood technology regardless of the consequences.
“I hope there’s no problem,” Trump said of Jensen Huang on Monday, but it seemed a little late for that. The problem is that the cofounder of the world’s most powerful and valuable AI company — and the closest adviser to the president on the technology — appears to have been hopelessly compromised by our chief adversary, China. As Stephen Witt, who wrote a book about Nvidia, told the New Yorker, “If the CEO is sleeping with spies, that’s generally regarded as bad.”
Worse, the president appears to have known that for some time, even though he persists in assurances that Huang is “a very high-quality,” “amazing,” and “honorable guy” who will end up “in good shape.” Trump was warned of Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset last year and again in May, the Times reported, just before the executive joined the president on a trip to Beijing.
And yet, Trump appears to have done nothing about it apart from enthusiastically facilitating the goals of a man who may have been in thrall to the Chinese Communist Party. Huang has somewhat paradoxically argued that the United States must maintain its chipmaking advantage over China by selling more chips to the country, which Trump helped him do by easing export controls established under President Joe Biden. The Commerce Department also reportedly abandoned an investigation into whether Alice Huang’s company smuggled chips into China after an Nvidia lawyer contacted the administration.
» READ MORE: Gov. Shapiro’s victory positions him as a formidable national force | Editorial
Nvidia is among the major investors in an estimated $1.4 trillion initial public offering being prepared by the AI company Anthropic, which has warned potential investors that the technology poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” And yet, Trump has hewed to the laissez-faire approach to AI that Jensen Huang has pushed, concluding after meeting with him and other tech executives that the companies should “self-police.”
Nvidia itself illustrates the folly of this notion. The company’s generally deferential board is populated by early investors and longtime associates of the cofounder, and — prior to Huang’s resignation — there was no succession plan or clear replacement. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will lead the company while the search for a permanent replacement commences.
Perhaps the only good that can come of all this recklessness is the thorough debunking of the irresponsible idea that such a powerful technology should go unregulated. Changing the current policy, or lack thereof, will certainly be challenging as long as Trump remains in power. But the new Congress is full of members elected on promises to rein in data centers and other aspects of AI, and, in some cases, with a history of doing so.
This mess shows they won’t arrive a moment too soon.
About our editorials
Editorials express an opinion about a matter of policy or public interest that has been researched and written by our Editorial Board, a group of journalists separate from the newsroom. Unlike news stories, which are fact-driven and written by reporters, editorials advocate, champion, argue, critique, and offer solutions. Editorials are not intended to dictate what readers should think, but to cut through the noise of polarized debate and provide a catalyst for elevated discourse.

sources.news_title: Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim CEO? Longtime exec takes top spot after Jensen Huang resigns
sources.text:
CHICAGO – Nvidia has appointed a 13-year veteran executive behind some of its biggest financing deals as interim CEO after the abrupt resignation of its longtime leader shook Silicon Valley.
With Jensen Huang stepping down over reports of extramarital affairs, including reportedly with a Chinese spy, Nvidia on Thursday turned to Colette Kress to take control. Kress is a high-ranking financial executive who regularly communicated with Wall Street analysts and investors as the company burgeoned into a $4 trillion linchpin in the artificial intelligence industry.
Recommended Videos
Kress has been a key architect of Nvidia's strategy of striking partnerships with and investing in companies that are also customers in what are referred to as “circular financing” deals. The arrangements have raised concerns about financial risk.
For example, Nvidia holds a nearly 13% stake in the neocloud company CoreWeave, which purchases Nvidia chips and rents out the computing power to companies developing AI models. When shares of Nvidia slid Thursday, CoreWeave shares plunged 7%.
The company also has financing deals with the AI lab OpenAI and the neocloud Nebius, among others.
Kress joined the California chipmaker in 2013 as executive vice president and chief financial officer. She takes over for Jensen Huang, known for his black-leather jacket, who became something of a global spokesman for the power of AI, whose sudden departure spooked Wall Street.
Shares have fallen more than 30% since the shares hit an all-time high in October, falling another 5% Thursday.
A singular figure in the tech world, Huang faced growing calls to step down after The New York Times reported on his relationship with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Late Wednesday, the paper and other outlets reported on another inappropriate relationship between Huang and another Nvidia executive who reported to him.
In a statement Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people" and that she would build on the "extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
Nvidia's high-end chips have become the building blocks used to build out AI. And in her CFO role, Kress was a key architect in financing deals with many of Nvidia's biggest customers that include AI titans from Anthropic to CoreWeave.
Yorkville Ives financial analyst Dan Ives said Thursday that he and his team are “big fans” of Kress, though he's not convinced that she will be Huang's permanent replacement.
“Colette Kress has built enormous credibility internally and externally,” Ives wrote, but there's a “good chance Nvidia's board looks to the outside for a CEO.”
Kress has a long resume in the tech world. Prior to joining Nvidia, she worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments in a variety of roles, according to an executive bio on the company’s website. She is a University of Arizona graduate with an MBA from Southern Methodist University.
Thanks to Nvidia’s soaring stock, Kress is one of the world’s wealthiest executives with a personal worth estimated by Forbes in June of over $1 billion dollars, though Nvidia shares have fallen by nearly third since then. She was awarded a pay package worth $14 million for Nvidia's fiscal 2026, according to Nvidia's proxy statement.
Nvidia did not directly address the extramarital affairs in Thursday’s announcement. But over the weekend, the company said it was investigating whether Huang was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort" — and the then-CEO separately apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. China’s Foreign Ministry has dismissed the spying allegations.

sources.news_title: The Nvidia Cheating Scandal Is Getting Messier
sources.text:
While we all wait around wondering which British hunk is going to be the next James Bond, might I interest you in some real-life espionage drama? On Sunday, Nvidia CEO and leather-jacket lover Jensen Huang acknowledged that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The company’s board of directors announced on Sunday that it was initiating an investigation following reporting that Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” On Thursday, Huang resigned from Nvidia following a report of a second affair, this time with an executive at the company. Here’s what you need to know.
Remind me what Nvidia does, please.
Nvidia’s main products are artificial-intelligence chips, technology that powers nearly all machine learning in the U.S. The company is currently valued at $3.96 trillion (down from over $4 trillion earlier this week) and is one of the major tech companies currently bolstering the U.S. economy. The export of Nvidia chips has been intensely restricted since 2022, when the U.S. began to push for dominance in the AI race.
How did a spy get involved?
Last month, the New York Times reported that the U.S. suspected that Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), an executive at a Singapore-based data-center company called Megaspeed, had given intelligence to China and possibly sent Nvidia AI chips to the country. A week later, the paper reported that Alice had been recruited as a spy by China’s Ministry of State Security in order to get close to Jensen and learn more about Nvidia’s top-of-the-line AI chips. It’s unclear when exactly Alice was purportedly recruited, but according to the Times, part of her mission was to influence Nvidia to advocate for its chips to be made available in China.
The timeline of Jensen and Alice’s relationship is also murky. The pair were photographed sitting next to each other at a tech-industry party in Taipei in June 2024, around the same time her company began purchasing what would wind up being billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips. In May 2025, they were filmed dining together with other execs at a restaurant in Taipei, and the Times reported that she gave him a kiss on the cheek. Before Nvidia announced its investigation, company spokesperson John Rizzo told the Times that interactions between his CEO and Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected” and that she was merely one of the “thousands of customer executives” he speaks with every year.
One thing we do know is that Alice was kind of obsessed with posting photos of her and Jensen to her social-media feeds. Apparently, he was all over her WeChat and Weibo pages. Is that good spycraft?
What did Nvidia say about all of this?
On Sunday, the company announced an independent investigation into Jensen allegedly being targeted by a spy. The Nvidia board said it has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”
In his own letter to the board, Jensen acknowledged having an extramarital affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he wrote. Huang said that he takes “full responsibility” for what he’s done and that he hopes he can “earn back” his family’s trust. He has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, and they have two grown children.
Huang also acknowledged the “national security concerns” in recent reports and promised that he is a good old-fashioned patriot. “I love our country and our company,” he said. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
Did President Trump know about this?
Yes, and he didn’t really care. Last year, President Trump — who has a close relationship with Jensen Huang — was reportedly briefed that Alice Huang was relaying information about Nvidia to Beijing but did nothing about it. This past spring, per the Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned Trump officials that Jensen was in a close relationship with Alice Huang. The memo arrived ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, where Jensen ultimately joined him, though the Times reported that he was not initially on the invite list. It’s unclear whether or not his exclusion was related to the memo.
Amid Jensen’s scandal, Trump is still riding for his pal. Speaking to reporters on Sunday night, the president said that the Nvidia CEO is an “honorable guy.” “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump said. The president added that Huang “probably had an excuse” and that he’s “done an amazing job for our country.” Of course, that was before the Times reported on a second affair.
What’s this about more cheating?
According to five sources who spoke to the Times, Jensen had a separate affair, though this one was less a matter of national security and more classically gauche. The Times reported on Wednesday that he had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care. Powell reported directly to Jensen. She is also married.
So is Jensen getting fired?
He can’t get fired, he quit! On Thursday, Jensen announced his resignation from Nvidia. In a press release, the company announced that executive vice-president and chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO. “Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” Kress said in a statement.
Does this mean I should scoop up some Nvidia stock?
Great question. The company’s stock took a nosedive following the news of Jensen’s departure, falling more than 10 percent at the NYSE opening bell. I am fairly certain that’s bad for them but maybe good for you? I don’t know; I zone out during the money parts of Industry.
This post has been updated.

sources.news_title: The Latest: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after his affair raises US security concerns
sources.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after his extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman who reportedly was also acting as a spy for Beijing raised U.S. national security concerns. The company named Colette Kress as interim CEO. She had been Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.
Huang’s resignation comes after Nvidia’s board gathered to discuss his future following revelations that he was having an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International suspected of spying for China. The two aren’t related.
Recommended Videos
The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. The Associated Press could not independently confirm those reports.
Shares of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world, fell sharply at the opening bell Thursday.
Here's the latest:
Huang leaving will end uncertainty for Nvidia
Some tech leaders have criticized the Nvidia board’s decision to oust Huang.
Elon Musk wrote in a post on X that it would be an “honor” to hire Huang.
But Bret Greenstein, the chief AI officer at global consultancy West Monroe, said the decision was necessary to end the uncertainty swirling around the company.
“The uncertainty of what would have come out next is probably the thing that would have hurt Nvidia, but also the market broadly for a longer period of time,” he said. “This is probably a clean break and a reset that allows everyone to sort of move to the next step rather than wondering what might fall next. Uncertainty is obviously bad for everybody. This created a moment where certainty will happen.”
___
Jeffries slams Trump’s push to install Tim Cook at Nvidia
It shows once again “this administration has repeatedly undermined the free market economy,” said the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to become speaker when the new Congress convenes in January.
“This is just another example of Donald Trump weighing in on behalf of his views connected to corporate America, as opposed to focusing on working class America,” Jeffries said.
___
Huang’s departure is a test for the AI industry
Stephanie Balaouras, group research director for research firm Forrester, said Jensen Huang’s resignation from chip-maker Nvidia isn’t just a test for the company but the AI boom as a whole.
“If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience. If its stock, financing relationships, or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI bubble ledger,” she said. “Tech leaders shouldn’t overreact, but they should treat Nvidia’s CEO transition as a prompt to reassess concentration risk across their AI infrastructure, suppliers, and investment plans.”
___
Singapore says US authorities weren’t helpful as it probed Megaspeed
Singapore said U.S. authorities weren’t helpful as the city-state investigated Alice Huang, Megaspeed International, and other companies over shipments of computer servers.
The Singaporean government said that as part of its investigation, it sought information from the U.S. and other jurisdictions to verify declarations it received from the companies.
Singapore singled out Supermicro, a U.S.-based server supplier, for information relevant to the investigation. But the company “provided limited cooperation” so the police and prosecutors raised the issue with U.S. authorities, issuing repeated requests since September 2025 to the Department of Justice and the FBI.
“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the government said.
___
US lawmakers still expect a briefing with Jensen Huang
U.S. lawmakers say they still want a briefing from Jensen Huang despite his resignation so that he can answer questions about his interactions with a Chinese businesswoman who reportedly was also acting as a spy for Beijing.
They also want to ask about the company’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage as well as other topics.
Rep. Brian Mast, chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, said the committee was in contact with Huang’s team as recently as Wednesday night about the interview. Lawmakers had made their initial request for the interview on Nov. 5. He also said that Huang would receive a subpoena, if necessary, to compel his appearance.
“They made their offer for what they would like to do, and we said, like in any negotiation, ‘no, this is what we’ll accept or your subpoena comes for the day after,’” Mast said.
Mast said Jensen has indicated a willingness to appear for the interview and that the committees involved in the inquiry wanted to see him “sooner rather than later.”
Nvidia shares fall after Huang’s resignation
Nvidia shares fell after the company announced Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO.
After tumbling at the open of trading, Nvidia shares were down 5.3% as of 10:30 a.m. EST Thursday.
The chipmaker became the face of the AI boom under Huang’s leadership. The shares set a record high last month after soaring an astounding 1,722% in four years. But Nvidia’s share price has dropped more than 30% since then, initially on concerns the enthusiasm over AI was overdone and this past week on worries about whether Huang would remain with the company.
The S&P 500 fell 0.4%, and technology stocks were the biggest weights dragging down the benchmark index. Nvidia and several other tech companies have pricey stock values that tend to have more influence on the market’s direction. The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.7%.
___
Trump says his close ally Huang ‘did a fantastic job’
President Donald Trump has reacted to the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang by saying that Huang “has done a fantastic job,” and adding, “There is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple.”
“A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote on his social media site of Cook, who is Apple’s former CEO.
Huang, who like a lot of top tech CEOs was close with Trump, left his post Thursday after his extramarital affair raised national security concerns. Huang faced growing calls to resign after his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Late Wednesday, media reports also said Huang had another extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee who reports to him. The FBI is investigating Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent.
___
A ‘watershed’ moment for Nvidia
Huang’s resignation is a watershed moment for Nvidia, said Asa Hiken, senior analyst for research firm eMarketer.
The chipmaker “now has to prove it can maintain its AI dominance without the leader largely responsible for building it,” Hiken said.
“Given the broader AI industry’s heavy dependence on Nvidia’s chips, Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself,” he said.
“While Huang’s personal decisions are scandalous, his particular affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises much bigger questions about the security risks facing companies at the center of the AI race,” he said. “AI technology has become critical to U.S. national security, making even the personal relationships of industry leaders a potential vulnerability.”
___
Ripping off ‘the band-aid’
Dan Ives, a technology analyst with the investment firm Yorkville Ives, said removing Jensen was a necessary step by the board of chipmaker Nvidia.
“The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past,” he wrote in a note to investors. “His value to the company pre- and post-this week is dramatically different, and the board did what we said it needed to do, which is rip off the band-aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter without him after this dark moment for Jensen and Nvidia.”
He still recommends investors buy Nvidia stock. He said Nvidia is still two to three years ahead of its nearest competitor and the “demand trajectory” for its chips isn’t changing because Jensen is gone.
___
Singapore says it has barred Alice Huang from returning to the country
Singapore authorities said Thursday that they banned Alice Huang from returning to the country after opening an investigation into Megaspeed over “suspected false declarations” about server purchases.
Investigators looked into whether servers were bought and exported through Singapore to neighboring Malaysia, and then routed to a final destination, contrary to what was declared in Singapore.
Police in the Southeast Asian city-state investigated Alice Huang for “suspected involvement in the possible offences,” but not for espionage, according to a detailed statement issued by the Home Affairs Department.
They seized her passport as part of investigation but returned it in February after concluding that “there was insufficient evidence” that she committed any offences.
But authorities gave her “a stern warning” and barred her from reentering the country because they suspected she “provided information which she knew to be inaccurate” to downplay her role at Megaspeed.
While the statement did not mention China or Nvidia, it said Singapore “does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate other countries’ export controls through fraud or dishonest practices.”
___
A plunge for Nvidia’s stock drags Wall Street lower
A plunge for Nvidia’s stock is pulling the U.S. market lower, threatening to upend the AI boom that has carried Wall Street to record after record in recent years.
The S&P 500 fell 0.7% Thursday. The weakness in AI stocks sent the Nasdaq composite down 1.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 127 points. Nvidia tumbled 14% after Jensen Huang, its co-founder and face of the brand, resigned as CEO. Other stocks in the AI industry also fell, though some of Nvidia’s rival chip companies rose. Oil prices swung after President Donald Trump said he’s no longer interested in a deal with Iran.
___
Megaspeed says it is committed to working with the US government
Megaspeed, the Singapore-headquartered data center company at the center of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal, pledged Thursday to cooperate with investigations into potential risks to U.S. national security.
“Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government,” said the statement signed by its chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan.
Nvidia has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Megaspeed faced claims last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports. Singapore has also said it is investigating such allegations.
China has denied that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, who heads one of the world’s most valuable companies. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump’s approval to sell its H200 chips to China.
___
Who is Alice Huang? The woman at the center of Nvidia’s scandal remains elusive
The explosive tale of Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang — involving marital betrayal, international intrigue and accusations of espionage — has rocked the tech and political worlds. Yet basic questions about her life — and how she grew close to one of the world’s most powerful technology executives — remain unanswered.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, drew wide attention last month, when The New York Times reported she had formed a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief and passed information to Beijing. U.S. officials, the Times reported, had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese spy who had been recruited to influence California-based Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China, a discovery the paper said set off alarms as high as the White House.
It remains unclear when the apparent affair started and when it might have ended. The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.
___
Who is Colette Kress?
Nvidia’s interim CEO is Colette Kress, who first joined the chipmaker back in 2013. She’s most recently served as the company’s executive vice president and CFO.
Prior to joining Nvidia, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments in a variety of roles, according to her executive bio on the company’s website.
In a statement Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she was “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
___
Shares of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world, plunged 10% in premarket trading
The company’s stock has been under pressure for weeks, both because of reporting about the affair and questions about a potential bubble in the AI sector.
Shares slid more than 7% to $160.85 before the opening bell, 34% below the company’s all-time high reached just over a month ago.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a second affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, and analysts said that may force the board to oust him.

sources.news_title: Why Nvidia turned to 'strategic' CFO Colette Kress to clean up Jensen Huang's mess
sources.text:
The saga of Jensen Huang, his reported two affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy has come to, if not an end, at least a pause. Huang resigned this morning as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaker he cofounded that is at the center of the global AI industry and made him a rock star CEO worth more than $140 billion. Stepping in to stop the bleeding as Nvidia’s share price falls is none other than Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO.
Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 and has been a key lieutenant at the company, with as much power as any exec might hope to have at a business that was run so completely by one man. (Huang reportedly had as many as 60 direct reports.) Before Nvidia, she held senior finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft. As Nvidia’s stock has soared over the past decade to a market cap that at its height surpassed $5 trillion, Kress has been a key face representing the company to Wall Street.
Now, she will become Nvidia’s interim CEO. The company’s board met on Wednesday evening and identified Kress to take over on an interim basis while it develops a permanent plan.
“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” Harvey Jones, the newly-installed chair of Nvidia’s board of directors, said in a statement. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap.”
The choice speaks to Kress’s influence at Nvidia. As questions swirled around Huang’s future, one was whether anyone could possibly take over the business that was so closely linked to him, personally. At least in the short term, Nvidia’s board decided Kress can.
She will remain CFO while serving as interim CEO. She said in her own statement that Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people.” And she reportedly told employees that she believes “deeply in this company.”
Kress has ranked on Fortune’s Most Powerful Women list for the past three years as Nvidia’s influence soared. (In 2026, she was No. 49—a position that reflected both her significant sway and the limits on it while Huang controlled the company so completely.) She is one of several women to serve as finance chiefs for AI businesses, from OpenAI to Meta to Alphabet. In May, Nvidia shared Kress’s ranking on the MPW list and said it reflected “the strategic role she plays in positioning our company as an innovator in AI and accelerated computing.” Her shares in Nvidia are currently worth approximately $770 million.
Kress reportedly told Nvidia staff the company would hold a meeting to discuss its future on Nov. 18, the day after it reports its third quarter financial results. She has been by Huang’s side as Nvidia transitioned from a niche player to one of the world’s most important companies, with influence over the global economy and national security. Now she will be at the helm as Nvidia wades through its next, unplanned, transition.

Wall St mixed as Nvidia chief's exit rattles AI stocks
sources.text:
Equities lower as Nvidia drop outweighs energy gains
US stocks have closed lower, as a drop in Nvidia shares after CEO Jensen Huang's exit outweighed gains in energy shares.
The chip company's shares fell but were well off the day's lowest level after earlier dropping nearly 12 per cent. Retail investors bought Nvidia shares worth about $111 million in the first half hour of trading, the biggest opening bid on record for the stock, according to data from Vanda Analytics.
The S&P 500 energy index rose for a fourth straight session as the best-performing of the 11 major S&P sectors. Crude prices climbed after President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the US did not need a deal with Iran.
Global AI-linked stocks fell and AI cloud firm Nebius tumbled after reporting its quarterly earnings and outlook. But Nvidia competitors such as Broadcom, Advanced Micro Devices, Alphabet and Amazon moved higher and were among the biggest boosts to the S&P 500.
Equities have been volatile in recent days. Sweeping Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have sparked investor concern about more AI regulation. Worries about Nvidia's leadership have also pressured one of the foundations of the current bull market. Nvidia tabbed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO.
"Right now, the market is selling AI stocks and tech stocks and buying safe stuff, just like it did in the first halo trade in January and February of this year, but it will flip back," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management in St Louis.
"That's the tug of war the market is doing right now. It's concerns about deceleration versus just pointing out that the absolute valuation and growth rates are still pretty compelling."
According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 25.99 points, or 0.34 per cent, to end at 7,593.39 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 102.44 points, or 0.40 per cent, to 25,363.75. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 190.29 points, or 0.36 per cent, to 52,296.20.
Even with Huang's departure, some investors expect questions to persist about the future of AI companies with strong ties to Nvidia.
The company has backed several firms, including its own customers, through financing arrangements that face greater scrutiny after Huang's departure.
"Nvidia is the circular-funder-in-chief; they're the biggest by far at this point, and I assume that activity will moderate," said Ellerbroek.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor index declined after surging 17.2 per cent over the prior four sessions.
Along with Nebius, peer CoreWeave dropped. Shares of data centre-related firms IREN and Applied Digital also slumped.
Investors are awaiting the release of the Producer Price Index on Friday, which will follow a hotter-than-expected consumer price reading earlier this week.
Markets are completely pricing in a December rate hike of at least 25 basis points by the Federal Reserve, with a 15 per cent chance of a 50-basis-point increase, according to CME FedWatch.
Comments from multiple Fed officials earlier this week suggested the US central bank was open to a more aggressive path of rate hikes as price pressures worsen.
Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said on Thursday she does not believe the central bank needs to shift to more aggressive rate hikes to combat inflation, while San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said she thinks the central bank will likely need to raise interest rates further to deal with elevated inflation, but did not suggest any urgency.

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang Quits Nvidia After Allegations Of Multiple Affairs
sources.text:
Jensen Huang Quits Nvidia After Allegations Of Multiple Affairs
Happy Thursday! It's November 12, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift — your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.
In this morning's edition we're looking at Jensen Huang leaving Nvidia, and global EV sales rising. We'll also look at Honda's hybrid plans for the U.S., and Stellantis' continued shutdown of its Fiat 500 plant.
If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.
1st Gear: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, has walked off into the sunset
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang cheated on his wife, allegedly with a Chinese spy. Nvidia was already spinning up investigations when that news broke, but new reporting alleges Huang also cheated with an employee at the company — one who reported to Huang himself. Now, Huang is out, and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is in the CEO chair in an interim role. From Nvidia:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Huang cofounded Nvidia, but he doesn't seem as integral to its operations as, say, Elon Musk is to SpaceX. The bigger issue Nvidia is facing right now is a lack of clear successorship, with no one sitting as heir apparent to the top spot — Huang planned to run the company himself for decades more before ever thinking of leaving, and he didn't exactly prepare anyone to take his place.
Kress, the CFO, is a logical interim replacement for the state of Nvidia right now: A financial house of cards built on circular financing and impossible valuations, moreso than a creator of cutting-edge computing hardware. What happens next, though — to both NVIDIA's automotive chipsets and its role in AI — is anyone's guess.
2nd Gear: EV growth is back up globally, despite flailing in the U.S.
EV sales are rough in the U.S. right now, and growth in China has tapered off. European sales, though, are still growing — and they're bringing the world up with them. Sales are climbing, despite our intent to go as backwards as possible. From Reuters:
Nov 12 (Reuters) – Global demand for electrified cars returned to growth in October, reflecting a very low US comparison base coupled with continued growth in Europe, data from UK-based research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence showed on Thursday.
"Even though the Chinese market is down domestically, that has then in turn resulted in a lot of OEMs pushing the exports and contributing significantly to the rest of the world," Benchmark data manager Charles Lester told Reuters.

It's going to be very interesting to see what happens with U.S. EVs over the next couple of years. Will the midterm "blue wave" propel us to government funding for EV infrastructure?
3rd Gear: Honda wants hybrids to bring it to 1.6 million U.S. sales
Honda wants to grow sales in the U.S., despite buyers' financial struggles, but it has a plan for how to marry those factors: Hybrids. The company thinks that, by making cars that save you on fuel, it'll make you more likely to spend upfront for one. From Automotive News:

The Fiat 500 is a fun little car, but we're not much in an era of fun little cars at the moment. As such, demand is low, and the Fiat 500 is selling so slowly as to make Stellantis idle its Italian manufacturing plant. From Reuters:

You'd think, with wages stagnating as costs increase, that people would return to cheap small cars. Have we really ceded so much of our souls to the C-HRs of the world that there's no room left for the humble Fiat 500?

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang Resigns as CEO of Nvidia After Affairs Revealed
sources.text:
By Tom Howell Jr. (The Washington Times)
Jensen Huang is stepping down as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaker he transformed from a gaming supplier into a $4 trillion behemoth at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom.
His resignation, announced by the company, follows revelations that he had affairs with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, and a company executive.
The discovery sparked investigations into whether the relationship with Ms. Huang compromised national security. Internal company pressure mounted after revelations he had a second affair with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported to him.
The Nvidia board said Colette Kress, an executive vice president and chief financial officer at Nvidia, will serve as interim CEO.
Ms. Kress said she is “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”
“We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders,” she said.
The company’s release said Mr. Huang, 63, had a “profound” impact and thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
Nvidia shares fell nearly 12% on the news, and stocks were down overall given the chipmaker’s prominent role in AI and the overall economy.
Mr. Huang, wearing his trademark leather jacket, had cultivated a close relationship with President Trump as part of negotiations around potential sales of Nvidia products to China.
China is the U.S.’ main rival in the AI race, so American officials are wary of giving Chinese companies access to advanced Nvidia chips.
U.S. lawmakers are probing whether Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang led to geopolitical problems.
Ms. Huang is a major shareholder in a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, so lawmakers want to know if she used the company to divert Nvidia products to China.
Megaspeed rejected allegations of illegal shipments to China and said Thursday it was committed to “working constructively and transparently” with U.S. investigators.
Megaspeed said it already cooperated with the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to work with any other relevant bodies.
“Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws,” the company said.
Last month, Mr. Trump honored Mr. Huang and other tech leaders with medals honoring achievements in science and technology.
Mr. Trump backed Mr. Huang after the affair revelations surfaced on Sunday.
He called Mr. Huang a “high-quality person” and said he wanted him to stay at the helm of Nvidia, considered the second-most valuable company in the world behind Apple.
“He said I had no idea that she was a spy, and I really, and I really believe him,” Mr. Trump said Monday. “I hope there’s no problem.”
This article was made available to WMAL via The Washington Times.

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang is out. The misogyny is forever.
sources.text:
Amid an ever-expanding scandal and plunging shares, Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO. The ouster of one of the most prominent figures in artificial intelligence comes after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair involving a woman the US government has identified as a possible spy for the Chinese government, as well as a subsequent damning report that he had carried out an affair with a direct report.
Yet, amid tanking stock prices, the lockstep support Huang enjoys with some of the world’s most powerful men is all but certain to remain intact. “That would be an honor,” Elon Musk wrote on Wednesday, responding to an online influencer’s plea for the trillionaire to hire Huang as news of the second affair emerged. Others like Bill Ackman called on the public to back the embattled leather-jacket enthusiast and “incredible human.” President Donald Trump, who has yet to comment on Huang’s resignation, on Monday called him a “high-quality guy,” brushing off reports that he, along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and multiple US national security officials, knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.
Online, the chorus of support took a distinctly misogynistic turn. Hundreds of commenters—many of them fake—posted photos snarkily comparing Huang’s wife of over four decades, Lori Huang, to Alice Huang, with whom he allegedly had an affair. The subtext throughout was clear: Jensen Huang’s longtime partner was no longer sufficiently attractive; affairs were justified. As one user wrote: “I don’t condone cheating, but the Jensen Huang situation is a reminder that women need to looksmax too. His wife literally looks like she could be his grandma.”
“Men are expected to make money, stay jacked, and look good forever. Women can’t just stop trying once they get the ring or you will force the man to upgrade!”
It’s as if the comments were saying what men like Trump could not, at least not publicly. But the rot goes far beyond its likely reflection of the private thoughts of powerful men. Together, they crystallized the support for a technology that regularly replicates their own sexism and gender bias. In fact, men like Musk and Trump have themselves uttered variations of the same misogyny. “Look at that face! Would anyone vote for that? Can you imagine that, the face of our next president?!” Trump once said of Carly Fiorina. Consider that numerous studies have shown that large language models are rife with misogyny, often treating women as sex objects and the property of men—ideas Musk has amplified on X. This technology is primarily led by men, designed by men, and is far more likely to be used by men. Now that one of their own has been caught in a sex scandal—one with deep national security implications—the support comes naturally.
That the president and Musk have yet to share one of these vile posts on their own social media accounts may be indicative of some kind of restraint. But their support for Jensen Huang, now a likely martyr in their eyes, may well grow louder.

sources.news_title: Jensen Huang steps down as CEO of Nvidia as suspected Chinese spy reportedly returns to Beijing
sources.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned as president, CEO, and board member effective immediately on Thursday following reports that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to consider his ouster, a person familiar with the matter said, after reports earlier in the day that the now-former CEO also had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.
Huang's exit plunges the $4 trillion company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped bankroll by pouring Nvidia's swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers, and the industry's biggest labs.
Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off.
The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang's push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump.
Trump said on Sunday that Huang had "done an amazing job for our country" and that the Nvidia chief had told him he had no idea the Chinese woman he had an affair with was a spy.
Who is Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal?
Much of Alice Huang's background is unconfirmed, but some details have been made clear in recent days.
The Chinese government has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, calling the allegations "purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
According to a Chinese private equity database site and a social media post by Shanghai Hexi Investment Management, Alice Huang began her career as a journalist at state broadcasters Hunan TV and CCTV before moving to finance, the Washington Post reported on Thursday.
However, there is no public record so far of Alice Huang working at either broadcaster.
Bai Jie, a former news anchor in China with over 2 million followers on Chinese social media platform Weibo, said Monday that she had known Alice Huang when they worked together as journalists and that Bai "already knew she was formidable back then,” according to the report.
Hours later, the post disappeared, and Bai denied making the statement. Bai's account was banned shortly afterward.
Alice Huang became deputy general manager of private equity firm Shanghai Hexi at some point in the 2010s and was also listed as a legal representative for tech firm Shanghai Longteng. When reporters from the Washington Post called Shanghai Longteng's publicly listed phone numbers, they were told they had the wrong number.
Huang's Megaspeed International begins buying Nvidia chips, raising suspicions
Alice Huang joined Megaspeed International, a little-known Singapore subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, in 2023; the company later spun off from its parent and pivoted to lending clients computing power from data centers powered by Nvidia chips, becoming one of the largest buyers of Nvidia's chips in Southeast Asia.
Megaspeed's success, with its assets growing from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, raised suspicions that the company was routing Nvidia's chips to China in violation of US export controls, according to The Washington Post report.
Citing US intelligence reports, The Washington Post wrote that Huang was tapped by the Ministry of State Security (MSS), Beijing’s spy agency, at some point and then began a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, but the timing remains unclear.
According to Bloomberg, the suspected Chinese spy has returned to Beijing. However, when or why she traveled to the capital is still unknown.

sources.text:
Nvidia Stock Plunges More Than 10% After Jensen Huang Resigns, Putting $400 Billion in Market Value at Risk
Nvidia CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board considers internal and external candidates for the permanent role
Nvidia shares plunged more than 10% on Thursday, 12 November, after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, a sell-off that threatened to wipe out more than $400 billion (£298 billion) of the chipmaker's market value in early trading.
The stock was down 11.9% from Wednesday's $173.73 (£129.43) close by 9:14 a.m. ET. After the open, it fell as much as 14%, its lowest since June 2025.
Bloomberg said the slide erased as much as $601 billion (£448 billion) in market value and pushed Nvidia below $4 trillion (£2.98 trillion) for the first time since 2025. If that holds at the close, it will be the largest one-day wipeout of market value for any stock on record.
Kress Takes Over With No Word From Huang
Huang's resignation as president, CEO, and director took immediate effect. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, at Nvidia since 2013, will serve as interim CEO while remaining finance chief. The board 'will consider internal and external candidates' for the permanent role.
Harvey C. Jones, a director since 1993 and former Synopsys chief executive, becomes Nvidia's first-ever chair. He said the board expects operations, customer commitments, and the product roadmap 'to continue without interruption.'
The announcement praised Huang's 'immeasurable contributions' but carried no comment from him or mention of the allegations.
From Spy Report to Resignation
The scrutiny began on 29 October, when The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials had concluded Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and former executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was passing information to Beijing.
According to the newspaper, surveillance over suspected chip diversion to China showed she had grown close to Jensen Huang, to whom she is not related, though officials initially believed he was unaware of her activities.
On Sunday, 8 November, Huang wrote in a memo to staff that did not name the woman, 'I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.'
The board opened an independent inquiry that day into reports he was 'the target of a foreign intelligence effort' but said it had 'confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.'
Shares fell as much as 8% on Monday. On Tuesday, independent directors hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and former federal prosecutor Joon H. Kim.
On Wednesday, the Times, citing five former employees, reported a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, who leads Nvidia's healthcare business and reports to Huang. Reached by phone, Huang said, 'I don't think you should be talking to me directly,' and hung up. Powell did not immediately respond.
The Wall Street Journal reported the board was preparing to remove him. The stock fell about 9% in after-hours trading, and directors met that night.
Analysts Slash Targets Before Earnings
Bernstein downgraded the shares to market perform and halved its price target to $200 (£149) from $400 (£298), writing, 'With the new allegations, it feels impossible to us for the board to keep him in the role.' Oppenheimer also downgraded the stock and pulled its target.
Nvidia reports third-quarter results on 17 November. Three Republican House committee chairs had asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on 18 November, and a class-action lawsuit in California federal court accuses Nvidia and Huang of inflating the share price by failing to disclose Huang's relationship.
